According to Homer, the dying Hector foretold that Achilles would be slain by Paris and Phoebus Apollo at the Scaean gate [1], and Thetis forewarned her son that he would perish beneath the wall of the Trojans by the swift missiles of Apollo [2]. responses_by_run.answer: Achilles withdrew from fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon because Agamemnon took his prize, Briseis. According to Homer's account, Achilles was angry that Agamemnon threatened to seize his war prize despite Achilles bearing the brunt of the fighting, while Agamemnon's own prize remained far greater [1]. Achilles declared he would return home to Phthia rather than remain dishonored and continue enriching Agamemnon through his efforts [1]. Apollodorus's account more simply states that Achilles did not go forth to war because he was angry on account of Briseis, the daughter of the priest Chryses [2].

responses_by_run.answer: Athena turned Arachne into a spider as punishment for her pride and defiance [1]. Arachne was a mortal weaver of extraordinary skill who refused to acknowledge Athena's superiority in the art of weaving [1]. When Athena, disguised as an old woman, advised Arachne to show humility and ask the goddess for pardon, Arachne scornfully rejected her and challenged the goddess to a weaving contest [1]. After they competed, Athena found Arachne's work flawless but was enraged by the mortal's skill and defiance [1]. Athena destroyed Arachne's web and struck her repeatedly [1]. Arachne then attempted to hang herself, but Athena saved her life while pronouncing a doom: 'your fate shall be to dangle on a cord, and your posterity forever shall take your example, that your punishment may last forever!' [2] Athena then sprinkled Arachne with a magical herb extract, transforming her body into that of a spider, condemning her to weave webs for eternity as an eternal punishment for her presumption [3].

Prometheus was punished for two main transgressions. First, he stole fire and gave it to humans [1]. According to Hesiod, Prometheus also attempted to deceive Zeus during a dispute over sacrificial portions at Mecone, dividing an ox unfairly by presenting Zeus with bones covered in fat while keeping the better portions for humans [2][3]. When Zeus learned that Prometheus had hidden fire in a fennel stalk and given it to humans, Zeus ordered Hephaestus to bind him to Mount Caucasus [1]. For these acts of defiance and deception against Zeus's will, Prometheus was subjected to eternal torment, with an eagle devouring his liver daily [1].

responses_by_run.answer: Odysseus escaped Polyphemus through a two-part plan. First, he blinded the Cyclops by sharpening a wooden club, heating it in fire, and driving it into Polyphemus's eye with the help of his comrades [1][2]. When Polyphemus cried out for help from other Cyclopes, they misunderstood his cries of "Nobody" and left him alone [1][2]. Second, after the blinding, Odysseus tied the Cyclops's rams together in groups of three and hid himself under the largest ram by clinging to its fleece [1][2]. When Polyphemus opened the cave door to let his flocks out to pasture, he felt the sheep as they passed but could not detect the men hidden beneath them [1][2]. Odysseus and his surviving comrades thus escaped with the sheep to their ship [1][2].

responses_by_run.answer: Perseus encountered several monsters during his adventures. The most notable was the Gorgon Medusa, whom he slew and beheaded [1]. Beyond Medusa, Perseus used the Gorgon's head as a weapon against other adversaries. He turned Phineus and his fellow conspirators to stone by displaying the Gorgon's head [2]. Similarly, he turned Polydectes and his gathered friends to stone by showing them the Gorgon's head with averted face [3]. Additionally, in the battle at Seriphus, Perseus encountered and slew various human warriors including Erithus (son of Actor), Caucasian Abaris, Polydaemon, Sperchius, Lycetus, Elyces, Clytus, and Phlegias, though these are warriors rather than monsters in the traditional sense [1].

Zeus's lineage traces back through several divine generations to Chaos itself. According to Hesiod's cosmological account, Earth (Gaia) emerged as a primordial deity [1], and from Earth came Cronus [2], who became Zeus's father. Cronus is attested across multiple sources: Hesiod presents him in his cosmological framework [2], Apollodorus includes him in his mythographic handbook [3], and Homer references him in both the Iliad and Odyssey as a figure of divine authority [4][5]. The Homeric Hymns also acknowledge Cronus's place in the divine genealogy [6]. Thus, the lineage flows from the primordial Chaos through Earth and Cronus to Zeus, establishing the Olympian king's descent from the cosmos's earliest divine forces.

Achilles' divine lineage to Zeus follows a clear patrilineal descent. Zeus begot Aeacus on the nymph Aegina [1]. Aeacus then fathered Peleus with Endeis, daughter of Sciron [1]. Peleus married the goddess Thetis, a Nereid, and together they became the parents of Achilles [1]. Thus Achilles traces his descent through his father Peleus to Aeacus, and through Aeacus directly to Zeus.

Homer's Iliad presents Achilles himself asserting this lineage, with Achilles stating: 'The father that begat me is one that is lord among the many Myrmidons, even Peleus, son of Aeacus; and Aeacus was begotten of Zeus' [2]. Ovid emphasizes the exceptional nature of Peleus' marriage to a goddess, noting that 'he was prouder of his father-in-law than of his grandsire' and that Peleus alone among his relatives 'was honored with a goddess for a wife' [3].
